frase_gancho.texto: A man reclining, his head turned to the side, carrying offerings to the gods.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the Chac Mool we move on to architecture. Step out into the hall’s garden and look for a temple that holds copies of some famous paintings, the ones the Maya made in the jungle of Chiapas.

guion_corto.texto: This limestone sculpture is more than a meter tall and almost a meter and a half long. It comes from Chichén Itzá, in Yucatán, and was made between the years nine hundred and twelve hundred. It is a Chac Mool: a man reclining on his back, with his knees bent and his head turned toward you. On his belly he holds a round vessel for offerings: copal, food, perhaps hearts. Notice the details: large square ear ornaments, a butterfly-shaped pectoral, sandals with heel guards. His face is oval, with a neutral expression that is hard to read. He is neither a god nor a king: he is thought to be a messenger between humans and the gods.

guion_largo.texto:
In the Toltec Hall I left you with a question: who influenced whom, Tula on Chichén Itzá, or Chichén Itzá on Tula? Here is the other side of it. This Chac Mool lives in the Maya world, more than a thousand kilometers from Tula, and it is very similar to the Toltec one. As if the question had no simple answer.

What we do know is that, around the year nine hundred, Chichén Itzá was an enormous city, with buildings that mixed Maya elements and elements from central Mexico. There stands the Temple of the Warriors, with its columns of warriors almost identical to those of Tula. And at the entrance or on top of several temples, a Chac Mool. Some think the Toltecs arrived; others, that it was an exchange between two powerful worlds; others, that Chichén was even older than Tula. Specialists are still debating, and perhaps more than one theory is right.

Think about what it did. That head turned sharply to one side looks as if it has just heard you approach. It stood at the entrance of a temple, to keep watch and to receive whoever arrived. And in the vessel on its belly they left copal, feathers, jade, food and, perhaps, sacrificial hearts. The figure was an intermediary: the one who carried the gifts of humans to the gods. Every offering passed through its hands. It is a gesture of service: it is not the god who receives, but the one who delivers, and that is why its body is always tense.

You already know the story of the name: Augustus Le Plongeon gave it in the nineteenth century, believing it was the portrait of a king. It was not, and we do not know what they called it. But the name stuck and today it is used for all sculptures of this type, from Tula to Yucatán.

And there are more to the west. In the West Hall you will see another Chac Mool, the one made by the Purépecha, carved in volcanic stone in what is now Michoacán. It is one of the most widely traveled images of ancient Mexico: from Tula to Yucatán, from Yucatán to the Templo Mayor, and from there to Michoacán. A way of reclining that everyone understood.

Chichén Itzá means something like “at the mouth of the well of the Itzá.” The well is a sacred cenote, into which offerings were thrown. Objects of jade, gold, copal and other treasures have been recovered there. It is a clue to how much water was worth, and how much was asked of it.

With this piece, the tour of the Maya Hall comes to a close, a tour that began with [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal) in the year 683. Between him and this Chac Mool, between two and five centuries passed, and many changes. Around the year nine hundred, several great cities of the southern Maya region were abandoned. But the Maya world went on, in the north, with Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán. And it continues today, with millions of people who speak Maya languages. It is not a mystery that vanished: it is a culture that endures.

texto: Look at the head: which way is it looking?
Observe the vessel it holds on its belly
Compare its posture with that of the Chac Mool in the Toltec Hall

texto.Discovery: 19th century, by Augustus Le Plongeon, at the Platform of Venus at Chichén Itzá

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Maya mysteriously disappeared after the year nine hundred.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Many cities in the south were abandoned, but the Maya world continued in the north. Today millions of people speak Maya languages.
